statutory presumption.act_source: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 / Section 139 NI Act
statutory presumption.formal_def: A mandatory legal inference that a court is bound to draw from a given set of established facts, shifting the evidential burden to the opposing party.
statutory presumption.simple_def: The law automatically assumes you are telling the truth from the start; the opponent must prove you wrong.
statutory presumption.analogy: Like an umpire ruling a batsman not-out — the judge assumes you are safe until the bowler produces clear camera evidence proving you wrong.
statutory presumption.example: When a signed cheque is produced, Section 139 NI Act presumes it was given for a genuine debt; the drawer must prove otherwise.

ratio decidendi.formal_def: The point in a case which determines the judgment, or the principle or rule of law upon which a judicial decision is founded.
ratio decidendi.simple_def: The core legal rule laid down by the court that all lower courts in the country must obey.
ratio decidendi.analogy: Think of a Supreme Court ruling as a permanent traffic light installed at a dangerous crossing — every driver (lower court) arriving there in the future must stop and obey that exact light.
ratio decidendi.example: In Bir Singh (2019), the ratio decidendi was that signing a blank cheque still binds the drawer under Section 139.

obiter dicta.formal_def: Remarks or opinions expressed by a judge in a court judgment that are incidental, non-binding, and unnecessary to the decision of the case.
obiter dicta.simple_def: Casual judicial remarks or advice mentioned in passing; helpful to read, but not legally enforceable.
obiter dicta.analogy: Like a sports commentator praising a player's haircut during a game — it's interesting commentary, but it doesn't count toward the match score.
obiter dicta.example: A judge remarking on general commercial ethics in a contract dispute without making it part of the final decree.

rebuttal.formal_def: Evidence or arguments introduced to counteract, refute, or destroy the presumption or evidence offered by the adverse party.
rebuttal.simple_def: Producing enough solid proof to break down and cancel out the other side's claim.
rebuttal.analogy: Like producing a dated GPS toll receipt when someone claims your car was parked in their driveway all afternoon.
rebuttal.example: Under Basalingappa (2019), showing the lender had zero bank withdrawal records successfully rebutted the Section 139 cheque presumption.

admission against interest.formal_def: A voluntary statement made by a party that is contrary to their legal or pecuniary interest, treated as substantive evidence against them.
admission against interest.simple_def: Any message, email, or signed letter where the other person admitted they owe you money or made a mistake.
admission against interest.analogy: Like a goalkeeper apologizing on live television for letting in an easy goal — they can't later argue in the locker room that the ball never crossed the line.
admission against interest.example: A WhatsApp chat where the debtor wrote 'I know I owe you ₹15 Lakhs, please give me two months' is an admission against interest.

section 63 bsa certificate.act_source: Section 63, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (formerly Sec 65B IEA)
section 63 bsa certificate.formal_def: A mandatory statutory certificate signed by a person in lawful control of a device certifying electronic secondary records for court admissibility.
section 63 bsa certificate.simple_def: The mandatory digital certificate needed to submit computer files, WhatsApp chats, or CCTV videos in court.
section 63 bsa certificate.analogy: Like a security boarding pass at an airport — without that stamped pass, airport security won't let you board the flight no matter how genuine your ticket looks.
section 63 bsa certificate.example: In Arjun Panditrao (2020), election video CDs were rejected because no official Section 63/65B server certificate was attached.

preponderance of probabilities.act_source: Indian Civil & Quasi-Criminal Standard of Proof
preponderance of probabilities.formal_def: The civil standard of proof requiring that a fact is proved if the court considers its existence more likely than its non-existence (51% probability threshold).
preponderance of probabilities.simple_def: Showing the judge that your version of events is more likely to be true than the other side's story.
preponderance of probabilities.analogy: Like a balanced scale where adding just one extra coin on your side tips the balance in your favour — you don't need a hundred coins, just 51% of the weight.
preponderance of probabilities.example: To defend against a cheque bounce case, the borrower only needs to raise probable doubt (51%), not prove total innocence beyond reasonable doubt.

condition precedent.formal_def: An act or event that must occur or be performed before a contractual right, statutory obligation, or court jurisdiction can take effect.
condition precedent.simple_def: A compulsory first step you must finish before you are legally permitted to take action or file a lawsuit.
condition precedent.analogy: Like inserting a coin into a vending machine before pushing the button — if you don't drop the coin first, pressing the button does absolutely nothing.
condition precedent.example: Sending a 30-day statutory demand notice is a condition precedent before filing a criminal complaint under Section 138 NI Act.

res judicata.formal_def: A doctrine preventing parties from relitigating a matter that has already been conclusively decided by a competent court on the merits.
res judicata.simple_def: You cannot sue someone a second time for the exact same dispute once the judge has already given a final decision.
res judicata.analogy: Like a coin toss before a cricket match — once the coin lands and the referee calls heads, you can't demand to flip it again just because you wanted tails.
res judicata.example: If a court dismisses your claim for land title after trial, you cannot file another suit in another city claiming the same title against the same person.

pendente lite.act_source: Code of Civil Procedure / Special Marriage Act
pendente lite.formal_def: Latin term meaning 'pending the litigation'; contingent on or active during the ongoing lawsuit.
pendente lite.simple_def: Temporary relief or monthly living expenses granted by the court while the main lawsuit is still going on.
pendente lite.analogy: Like an umbrella handed to you during a rainstorm — it protects you from getting soaked while you wait to reach shelter (the final judgment).
pendente lite.example: The court awarding ₹25,000 monthly maintenance pendente lite to a spouse until the final divorce case is settled.

ex parte.act_source: Order IX Rule 6, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
ex parte.formal_def: A proceeding conducted or an order passed in the presence of only one party, typically because the other party failed to appear after summons.
ex parte.simple_def: When the opponent ignores court notices and does not show up, the judge hears your side alone and passes an order.
ex parte.analogy: Like winning a boxing match by walkover because the opponent never stepped into the boxing ring when the bell rang.
ex parte.example: The court passed an ex parte decree against a builder who repeatedly refused to accept summons or attend consumer forum hearings.

prima facie.formal_def: Latin term meaning 'at first sight'; evidence that is sufficient to establish a fact unless disproved or rebutted.
prima facie.simple_def: On first look, the evidence seems genuine and convincing enough to proceed.
prima facie.analogy: Seeing black smoke pouring out of a building's window — at first glance, it looks like a fire, even before fire investigators inspect the kitchen.
prima facie.example: Producing a dishonoured cheque and a postal return receipt establishes a prima facie case under Section 138 NI Act.

adverse possession.formal_def: A legal principle whereby a person who occupies someone else's real property continuously and hostily for 12 years may acquire lawful ownership.
adverse possession.simple_def: If someone lives on private land openly without permission for 12 years and the true owner never objects, the occupant can claim ownership.
adverse possession.analogy: Like leaving a bicycle unlocked on a street corner for ten years — if you never claim it, the neighbour who parked it in their shed eventually treats it as theirs.
adverse possession.example: A landowner losing ownership of an agricultural plot because a tenant farmed it openly for 14 continuous years without interruption.

mesne profits.formal_def: Profits which a person in wrongful possession of property actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received, payable to the rightful owner.
mesne profits.simple_def: Compensation or rent the illegal occupant must pay you for the entire time they unlawfully stayed in your property.
mesne profits.analogy: If a stranger unlawfully takes your taxi and drives it for a month, they must pay you all the taxi fares they earned during that month.
mesne profits.example: A tenant who refused to vacate after lease expiry ordered to pay ₹50,000 per month as mesne profits to the landlord.

mens rea.formal_def: The mental element of an offence; the guilty intention or knowledge of wrongdoing that must accompany a criminal act.
mens rea.simple_def: A criminal mind or bad intention — the deliberate plan to cheat or commit a crime.
mens rea.analogy: Accidentally taking someone else's black umbrella from a restaurant stand isn't theft, but deliberately swapping your broken umbrella for their new one is.
mens rea.example: To prove criminal cheating under Section 318 BNS / 420 IPC, you must prove the borrower had dishonest intention right from the day they took the loan.

quashing.act_source: Section 528, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Sec 482 CrPC)
quashing.formal_def: The exercise of inherent judicial power by a High Court to completely strike down or annul an unlawful FIR, charge sheet, or criminal proceeding.
quashing.simple_def: The High Court completely tearing up and cancelling a false or frivolous criminal police case.
quashing.analogy: Like an exam examiner finding that a question was printed by mistake and cancelling it completely from every student's score sheet.
quashing.example: The High Court quashed an FIR for cheating because the dispute was purely a civil business disagreement over delayed delivery.

injunction.formal_def: A judicial order restraining a party from commencing or continuing a wrongful act, or compelling them to restore a previous condition.
injunction.simple_def: A court order that forces someone to immediately stop doing something (like demolition or selling a house).
injunction.analogy: Like a referee blowing a whistle and showing a red card to immediately stop a player from tackling an opponent.
injunction.example: A temporary injunction restraining a developer from constructing over a boundary line until property ownership is decided.

caveat emptor.act_source: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 / Consumer Protection Act, 2019
caveat emptor.formal_def: Latin maxim meaning 'let the buyer beware'; the principle that the buyer alone is responsible for checking the quality of goods before purchasing.
caveat emptor.simple_def: The buyer must inspect what they are buying before paying; you cannot complain later about obvious defects you should have noticed.
caveat emptor.analogy: Like buying fruit at a grocery stall — if you pick a bruised mango yourself and pay for it, you can't blame the shopkeeper for your choice.
caveat emptor.example: Under the Consumer Protection Act, this rule is now restricted by strict product liability on manufacturers.

unilateral appointment of arbitrator.act_source: Section 12(5) read with Seventh Schedule, Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
unilateral appointment of arbitrator.formal_def: The nomination of a sole arbitrator by one party having an interest in the outcome, rendered de jure ineligible under Indian law.
unilateral appointment of arbitrator.simple_def: One company picking their own referee to judge a match between themselves and their opponent — strictly illegal in India.
unilateral appointment of arbitrator.analogy: A cricket captain deciding that their own team coach will be the sole umpire for the final match.
unilateral appointment of arbitrator.example: In Perkins Eastman (2019), the Supreme Court struck down a PSU Managing Director's right to unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator.

liquidated damages.formal_def: A genuine pre-estimate of loss agreed upon by parties in a contract, payable as reasonable compensation in the event of breach.
liquidated damages.simple_def: A pre-agreed penalty amount written into a contract in case one side breaks their promise.
liquidated damages.analogy: Like a flight cancellation fee printed on your ticket — both you and the airline know in advance exactly what it costs to cancel.
liquidated damages.example: In Kailash Nath (2015), the Supreme Court held that Section 74 allows reasonable compensation only for actual loss proved to have occurred.

acknowledgment of debt.formal_def: An admission of existing liability made in writing and signed by the debtor before expiration of limitation, resetting the statutory clock.
acknowledgment of debt.simple_def: A written note, email, or balance sheet signed by the borrower acknowledging the debt, which restarts your 3-year filing deadline.
acknowledgment of debt.analogy: Like pressing the 'Snooze' or 'Reset' button on a 3-minute kitchen timer — it restarts the full countdown from zero.
acknowledgment of debt.example: In Asset Reconstruction Co. (2021), a borrower's signed annual balance sheet listing a loan reset the limitation clock under Section 18.
